prompt: What does an open-weight model give you that a closed one does not?
hint: Sort by what you are given.

choices.text: A lower price per token at every host that serves it
choices.why: Section 05 shows open models at a wide range of prices, some above closed ones' cheaper tiers.

choices.text: Freedom from any licence terms
choices.why: Open-weight weights come under a licence with conditions; that is what makes them open-weight rather than open source.

choices.text: The weights
choices.why: Right. You can download and run them yourself.

choices.text: Better answers than a closed model of the same size
choices.why: Openness says nothing about quality; lesson 5 measures that.

prompt: Llama 3.1's grant calls the licence 'non-exclusive, worldwide, non-transferable and royalty-free limited'. Which kind of model does that make it?
hint: Limited by what?

choices.text: Closed, because Meta keeps the rights
choices.why: You download and run the weights; a closed model never gives you them.

choices.text: Open-weight: the weights are yours to run, with conditions
choices.why: Right. 'Limited' is where the conditions of section 03 come in.

choices.text: Open source, because it charges no royalties to anybody who uses it
choices.why: Free of royalties is not free of conditions.

choices.text: Public domain, as it is worldwide
choices.why: Worldwide says where the permission applies, not that there is no owner.

prompt: The Open Source Initiative's definition of open-source AI asks for more than open weights. What does it add?
hint: What would somebody need to rebuild the model?

choices.text: A promise that the model will never be retired
choices.why: Retirement is about hosted names; the definition is about what is published.

choices.text: A free hosted endpoint for everybody
choices.why: Hosting is a service, not part of what makes a model open.

choices.text: A benchmark table in the model card
choices.why: Benchmarks describe performance; they do not let anyone rebuild anything.

choices.text: The training code and enough information about the data to rebuild it
choices.why: Right, and few released models meet it.

prompt: When is the 700-million-user threshold in Llama 3.1's licence measured?
hint: Read the first words of the clause.

choices.text: On the release date of that Llama version
choices.why: Right, so the clause cannot be grown into by accident.

choices.text: Every month, for as long as you use the model
choices.why: The clause fixes the count on the release date.

choices.text: When you first download the weights
choices.why: The download date is not mentioned.

choices.text: At the end of each calendar year, from your company's annual report
choices.why: The clause counts monthly active users in the month before release.

prompt: ana wants to generate training examples with a Qwen model under the Tongyi Qianwen licence and use them to fine-tune a Llama. What does clause b say?
hint: Output used to improve which model?

choices.text: It is allowed if Lantern Books has under 100 million users
choices.why: The user threshold is a different clause; b forbids this use at any size.

choices.text: Not allowed, whatever the size of the shop
choices.why: Right. Outputs are reserved for improving Qwen itself; Llama 3.1's licence allows this use, Qwen's older one does not.

choices.text: It is allowed if the Llama is renamed to start with Qwen
choices.why: Renaming is a Llama obligation, and it does not lift Qwen's ban.

choices.text: The licence says nothing about outputs
choices.why: Clause b is exactly about outputs.

prompt: Which of these trigger the distribution obligations in Llama 3.1's licence? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who is distributing the model, or a product containing it?

choices.text: Shipping an app that bundles the weights
choices.why: Yes: that is distributing a product that contains them.

choices.text: Offering a hosted Llama to your own customers
choices.why: Yes: that makes the model available to others.

choices.text: Calling a Llama through a host's API for internal sorting
choices.why: Using somebody's service is not distributing the model.

choices.text: Reading the model card
choices.why: Reading obliges you to nothing.

prompt: Put section 03's way of reading a model licence in order.
hint: Start with what you may do.
items: Any threshold, and when it is measured
The use policy, against your product
trap: The use policy comes last because it is read against what your product does, once you know the rest applies.

prompt: DeepSeek-V3's repository shows an MIT badge. What does MIT cover there?
hint: The README names two licences.

choices.text: The code and the weights alike
choices.why: The weights are under the separate Model License.

choices.text: The code
choices.why: Right. The models are under the Model License.

choices.text: The weights only, while the code is proprietary
choices.why: It is the other way round.

choices.text: The paper describing the model
choices.why: The README does not mention the paper's licence.

prompt: Which licence applies to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, according to R1's README?
hint: Where did the 8B distill start?

choices.text: MIT, like R1 itself
choices.why: R1 is MIT; the distill started as a Llama and keeps the Llama licence.

choices.text: DeepSeek's Model License, like V3
choices.why: V3's licence is not involved.

choices.text: The Llama 3.1 licence, from the base it was derived from
choices.why: Right. A derivative keeps its base model's licence.

choices.text: None, because distillation creates a new model
choices.why: The README says plainly that it is derived and keeps the original licence.

prompt: A team checks the licence file of a model's inference repository, finds Apache 2.0, and ships the weights in its product. What did they miss?
hint: What does an inference repository contain?

choices.text: That file licenses the code; the weights have their own licence, stated per model
choices.why: Right. Find the licence of the weights you will run.

choices.text: That Apache 2.0 forbids shipping in commercial products
choices.why: It allows commercial use.

choices.text: That inference code may only run on the maker's hardware
choices.why: Nothing ties it to particular hardware.

choices.text: Nothing; a repository has one licence
choices.why: DeepSeek-V3's has two, and says so.

prompt: In section 05's capture, Llama 3.3 70B costs $0.135 per million input tokens at the cheapest host and $0.90 at the dearest. How many times the cheapest is the dearest? Answer to one decimal place.
hint: Divide.

prompt: Why does one open model show a wide spread of prices while one closed model shows nearly one price?
hint: Who is allowed to serve each?

choices.text: Closed models are cheaper to run
choices.why: The cost of running is not what sets the closed price.

choices.text: Anybody is free to serve open weights, so hosts compete
choices.why: Right. For a closed model every route resells the maker's model.

choices.text: The sheet only records list prices for closed models
choices.why: It records both kinds the same way.

choices.text: Regulators fix the price of closed models in each region they are sold in
choices.why: The regional differences come from the clouds' routes, not from a regulator.

prompt: Two hosts list the same open model; one has 'fp8' in its entry and is cheaper. Before choosing it on price, what should ana check?
hint: What does fp8 change?

choices.text: Whether the host accepts payment in reais
choices.why: Payment is a detail; the weights themselves differ.

choices.text: Whether fp8 is a newer version of the model
choices.why: It is the same model at reduced precision, not a new version.

choices.text: Her own cases, since reduced precision alters the numbers
choices.why: Right. Same name, different numbers; measure before trusting the price.

choices.text: Nothing, because a host is not allowed to modify the weights it serves to customers
choices.why: Serving at reduced precision is common and allowed.

prompt: What happens to a request that names a closed model identifier after its retirement date?
hint: It stops answering.

choices.text: It is silently answered by the newest model in the family
choices.why: That is what an alias does; a retired dated identifier returns an error.

choices.text: It gets an error instead of a reply
choices.why: Right, which is why the date goes in a calendar.

choices.text: It keeps working, at a higher price
choices.why: Retirement ends service; it is not a price change.

choices.text: It is queued until the provider restores the model
choices.why: Retired models are not restored.

prompt: Match each kind of model name to how it changes.
hint: Section 06's two bullets, and the file on disk.

pairs.right: Never changes, and one day stops answering
Keeps answering; what answers can change

pairs.left: Weights in a file on your disk
pairs.right: Changes only when you replace the file

right_distractors: Changes every time the price changes

prompt: ana evaluated her cases against an alias rather than a dated identifier. Three months later accuracy drops with no change on her side. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What does an alias point at?

choices.text: The alias now points at a different model
choices.why: Right. Pin a dated identifier, and re-run the cases when it moves.

choices.text: The cases wore out from being used too often
choices.why: Cases do not wear out; the model under the name changed.

choices.text: The model's knowledge cutoff moved backwards
choices.why: A cutoff belongs to a model and does not move.

choices.text: The provider started charging her account more for each request she makes
choices.why: Price does not change accuracy.

prompt: With open weights served by a third-party host, where does the customer's e-mail go?
hint: Who runs the machine?

choices.text: Nowhere: open weights keep data in
choices.why: Only when you run them yourself.

choices.text: To the model's makers, who receive a copy from every host
choices.why: Nothing in a licence sends requests to the makers.

choices.text: To the host, under the host's terms
choices.why: Right, as it would to a closed provider.

choices.text: To the nearest public cloud
choices.why: It goes to whoever runs the host's machines.

prompt: Section 07's capture prices Claude Sonnet 5.5 input at $2 per million tokens on Bedrock's global route and $2.20 on the eu. route. What is the regional premium, in per cent?
hint: The difference over the global price.

prompt: A contract says customer e-mails may not be processed outside the European Union. Which option satisfies it with a closed model?
hint: Section 07's four routes.

choices.text: The global route, because it is cheapest
choices.why: Global may send the request wherever there is capacity.

choices.text: Any route, as long as the account is registered in Europe
choices.why: Where the account is registered does not decide where requests run.

choices.text: None: closed models cannot be kept in a region
choices.why: The clouds sell exactly that, at a premium.

choices.text: An EU-only route, at its premium
choices.why: Right. The ten per cent buys a guarantee about geography.

prompt: Match each licence clause to the licence that carries it, as quoted in this lesson.
hint: Sections 03 and 04.

pairs.left: No outputs to improve other LLMs
Use-based restrictions carried by every derivative

prompt: A model name ending in -latest is an ___: it keeps answering, and what answers may change.
hint: Section 06's second bullet.

prompt: Which consideration in this lesson is the one open weights win outright, whoever hosts them?
hint: Hosted open weights share the closed models' answer on data.

choices.text: The data never leaving your systems
choices.why: Only when you run them yourself; a host receives the data.

choices.text: A lower price per token
choices.why: Some hosts are cheap, some are not; it depends on the host.

choices.text: Deciding when the model changes
choices.why: Right. If a host drops it, you still hold the weights and take them elsewhere.

choices.text: Freedom from licence conditions
choices.why: Open-weight models carry conditions by definition.
